old.name: DO Empordà reds
old.hook: Garnatxa and carinyena grown on slate and tramuntana wind, in Spain's north-easternmost DO.
old.text: The DO was founded by Spanish order of 19 May 1975 (originally 'Empordà–Costa Brava'; the coast name was dropped and the zone widened into the Baix Empordà in 2006). Black grapes run to carinyena negra, garnatxa negra — locally lledoner — plus cabernet, merlot, syrah and ull de llebre; garnatxa alone covers roughly a third of the DO's ~1,768 ha. The wind keeps the vines low and the yields small.

old.name: Garnatxa de l'Empordà
old.hook: The sun-dried sweet garnatxa you drink after dinner — a protected style, not a separate DO.
old.text: A traditional style inside the DO Empordà regulation, at least ~90% garnatxa. Technique: grapes are left to over-ripen and dry (the raïm assolellat / sun-dried method), harvested late — traditionally the third week of September — to concentrate sugar to around 14–15% potential alcohol before the ferment is arrested. Warm, raisined, generous. The Espolla cooperative is the classic source.

old.name: Vi novell
old.hook: The season's first wine, tapped around Sant Martí on 11 November.
old.text: 'Per Sant Martí, mata el porc i enceta el vi' — for Saint Martin, kill the pig and broach the wine. Technique: a few weeks of aging, no more, bottled to keep the fruit and a faint natural spritz from the ferment. Drunk young and festively in the weeks after the November release; the Espolla cooperative bottles a well-known one within the DO Empordà.

old.name: Vermut de l'Empordà
old.hook: An Empordà vermouth built on the native garnatxa roja, not the Reus tradition.
old.text: Celler Gerisena in Garriguella makes 'Obreboques', a vermouth on garnatxa roja — a native Empordà variety — aged two years in oak, framed by its makers as an Empordà terroir drink rather than a copy of the Reus/Barcelona style. The Sunday-noon vermut before lunch is the ritual it belongs to.

old.name: Ratafia catalana
old.hook: Green-walnut-and-herb liqueur — an EU-protected spirit GI, with its festival at Santa Coloma de Farners.
old.text: Registered as a geographical indication under Regulation (EC) 110/2008. The spec: a hydroalcoholic maceration of green walnuts (min. 10 g/l) for at least three months with aromatic herbs, 24–30% ABV, aged a minimum three months in wood. Home practice picks the walnuts green in June–July and macerates them in the sun for about forty days. Santa Coloma de Farners, in Girona province, is its cultural capital — the Festa de la Ratafia ran its 44th edition in 2025.

old.name: Cremat
old.hook: Rum set alight with coffee, cinnamon and lemon — the drink of the havanera nights.
old.text: A flambéed mix of rum, sugar, cinnamon stick, lemon peel and coffee, burned off before serving; the Cuban rum and the havanera songs both came home with sailors from the Antilles trade. Technique: it is stirred in its own flames for several minutes before being doused with coffee. Calella de Palafrugell's Cantada d'Havaneres, the first Saturday of July, is where it is drunk communally and hot.

old.name: 'La Santa Espina' — Enric Morera
old.hook: The sardana that became a banned anthem.
old.text: Composed by Enric Morera to a text by Àngel Guimerà, premiered 1907; the most emblematic Catalan sardana, banned under both the Primo de Rivera and Franco dictatorships. If a cobla strikes it up in Plaça de la Independència, the older dancers will rise first.

old.name: Nits de Clàssica in the nave
old.hook: Chamber music under the widest Gothic vault.
old.text: The city's festival puts violinists and pianists inside the Cathedral, its cloister and Sant Pere de Galligants — stone that turns a solo line vast. Hearing Bach under the 22.98 m vault is the closest thing Girona has to a house sound.

old.name: 'El meu avi' — the havanera
old.hook: The 1968 song that ends every Costa Brava night.
old.text: Written in 1968 and the best-known havanera, it has closed the Cantada d'Havaneres de Calella de Palafrugell every year since 1977 — sung over a cremat, the whole square joining the last verse about a grandfather's boat lost off Cuba.

old_also.name: Havaneres & cremat
old_also.hook: Cuban song brought home by returning sailors.
old_also.text: The habanera crossed back to the Costa Brava with the men who worked the 19th-century Cuba trade — slow, salt-worn songs sung to guitar and accordion, always with a pot of flaming rum-and-coffee cremat going. The genre the coast made its own.
